chunks: Design a system to test X. The question: Design a system to test x.
"Design a system to test X" has no answer until you ask what X is and what the test must prove. So begin with questions: how many units, how fast, how accurate, and where it runs.
Then turn the spec into measurements with pass limits, and build a setup that applies inputs, measures and logs results.
Think of a driving test. The examiner follows a fixed checklist with clear pass limits. Every candidate gets the same route and the same conditions, and each result is recorded.
If the rules were vague or the route changed daily, passing would mean nothing. A hardware tester must likewise be repeatable, fast enough for the line, and trustworthy.
The controller drives every instrument. Stimulus (supply, load) and measurement (DMM, scope through the relay matrix) meet at the fixture.
Results are logged against the DUT serial number, so failures can be traced and yield tracked.
DUT: device under test, the product being checked. Fixture: the plate with spring-loaded pins that connects the DUT to the instruments.
Kelvin (4-wire) sensing: separate pins for forcing current and for measuring voltage, so contact resistance does not corrupt the reading.
Guard band: test limits tightened by the measurement uncertainty, so a passing unit really is in spec. Throughput: how many units per hour the station can test.
Golden unit: a known-good DUT used to check the tester itself.
Test a 3. 3 volts board with a limit of ±3%, which is ±99 millivolts. Spring-loaded (pogo) pins can add about 50 milliohms of contact resistance. At 1 amps that drops 0.
05 times 1 equals 50 millivolts. That is half the allowed window, so use Kelvin sensing. Time budget: 15 test points at 0.
8 seconds each, plus 6 seconds of handling, is 18 seconds per board. That is 3600 over 18 equals 200 boards per hour.
A script runs the tests, compares each result to limits in a file, and logs it by serial number.
Check the tester with a golden unit that must pass and a known-bad unit that must fail. That is the whole idea.
"I'd start by asking what X is and what the test must prove, volume, cycle time and accuracy.

Then I'd define the tests and limits from the spec, and build a fixture with Kelvin contacts, programmable supply and load, a DMM and scope controlled by a script that sequences the tests, applies limits and logs results by serial number.
I'd choose instruments about four times more accurate than the limits, set guard bands, and validate the tester with golden and known-bad units."
Quick check. What should you do first when asked to design a test system for X?
